title: Celsus recants and urges courting rulers
source_text: Κέλσος μὲν ουν οἶμαι μετὰ τοσούτους, οὓς εἶπε περὶ δαιμόνων δεομένων κνίσσης καὶ αἵματος λόγους, ὡσπερεὶ ἐπὶ μοχθηρίαν ἐρχόμενος παλινῳδίαν φησὶν ὅτι μᾶλλον οἰητέον τοὺς δαίμονας μηδενὸς χρῄζειν μηδὲ δεῖσθαί τινος ἀλλὰ χαίρειν τοῖς τὸ εὐσεβὲς δρῶσι πρὸς αὐτούς. ἐχρῆν δ᾿, εἰ τοῦτο ᾤετο εἶναι ἀληθὲς. ἐκεῖνα αὐτὸν μὴ τεθεικέναι, ταῦτα ἀπηλειφέναι. ἀλλὰ γὰρ οὐ πάντῃ ἡ ἀνθρωπίνη φύσις ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τῆς μονογενοῦς αὐτῷ ἀληθείας καταλείπεται. διόπερ καὶ Κέλσος εἶπε μὲν ἐν τῷ περὶ κνίσσης καὶ αἵματος, ὧν χρῄζουσι δαίμονες. τἀληθῆ· πάλιν δ᾿ ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας κακίας κατώλισθεν ἐπὶ τὰ ψευδῆ καὶ ἐξομοιοῖ τοὺς δαίμονας ἀνθρώποις τοῖς τελέως δικαίως πράττουσι τὰ δίκαια. κἂν μηδεὶς αὐτοῖς γινώσκῃ χάριν. τὰ ἀγαθὰ δὲ ποιοῦσι τοῖς ἀμειβομένοις τὸ εὐχάριστον. δοκεῖ δέ μοι συγχεῖσθαι κατὰ τὸν τόπον καὶ ὁτὲ μὲν τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν ὑπὸ τῶν δαιμόνων ταράττεσθαι, ἔσθ᾿ ὅτε δὲ καὶ ἀνανήφων ἀπὸ τῆς ὑπ᾿ ἐκείνοις ἀλογιστίας ἐπ᾿ ὀλίγον τι βλέπειν τοῦ ἀληθοῦς. πάλιν γὰρ ἐπιφέρει· θεοῦ δὲ οὐδαμῇ οὐδαμῶς ἀπολειπτέον οὔτε μεθ᾿ ἡμέραν οὔτε νύκτωρ οὔτ᾿ ἐς κοινὸν οὔτ᾿ ἰδίᾳ λόγῳ τε ἐν παντὶ καὶ ἔργῳ διηνεκῶς. ἀλλά γε καὶ μετὰ τῶνδε καὶ χωρὶς ἡ ψυχὴ ἀεὶ τετάσθω πρὸς τὸν θεόν. ἐγὼ δ᾿ ἀκούω τοῦ μετὰ τῶνδε τουτέστι μετὰ τοῦ κοινοῦ καὶ μετὰ παντὸς ἔργου καὶ μετὰ παντὸς λόγου. εἶτα πάλιν ὡσπερεὶ παλαίων τῷ λογισμῷ πρὸς τὰς ἀπὸ τῶν δαιμόνων ἐκστάσεις καὶ τὰ πολλὰ νικώμενος ἐπιφέρει καὶ λέγει· εἰ ὧδε ἔχοιεν, τί τὸ δεινὸν τοὺς τῇδε ἄρχοντας εὐμενίζεσθαι, τούς τε ἄλλους καὶ τοὺς ἐν ἀνθρώποις δυνάστας καὶ βασιλέας, ὡς οὐδὲ τούτους ἄνευ δαιμονίας ἰσχύος τῶν τῇδε ἠξιωμένους; ἐν μὲν οὖν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω κατῆγεν ὅσον ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτῷ τὴν ψυχὴν ἡμῶν πρὸς τοὺς δαίμονας· νῦν δὲ βούλεται ἡμᾶς ἐξευμενίζεσθαι καὶ τοὺς ἐν ἀνθρώποις δυνάστας καὶ βασιλέας, ὧν ἐπεὶ μεστὸς ὁ βίος καὶ (αἱ) ἱστορίαι, νῦν οὐχ ἡγησάμην ἀναγκαῖον ἐκθέσθαι τὰ παραδείγματα.
pass_a_gloss: Celsus, I think, after so many words (λόγοι) which he said about demons needing (δέομαι) savour and blood, as though coming to wickedness (μοχθηρία), says a recantation (παλινῳδία), that one must rather think the demons need (χρῄζω) nothing nor lack (δέομαι) anything but rejoice (χαίρω) in those doing the pious thing (τὸ εὐσεβές) toward them. He ought, if he thought this true, not to have set down (τίθημι) those things, [or] to have erased (ἀπαλείφω) these. But human nature (ἀνθρωπίνη φύσις) is not wholly (πάντῃ) abandoned (καταλείπω) by God and the only-begotten (μονογενής) truth to Him. Therefore Celsus too said the true things in the passage about savour and blood, which demons need; but again by his own wickedness (κακία) slid down (καταλισθάνω) to the false things (τὰ ψευδῆ) and likens (ἐξομοιόω) the demons to men perfectly (τελέως) justly (δικαίως) doing just things, even if no one is grateful (χάριν γινώσκω) to them, but doing good things to those repaying (ἀμείβομαι) gratitude (τὸ εὐχάριστον). He seems to me to be confused (συγχέω) about the subject and at times his ruling faculty (τὸ ἡγεμονικόν) is troubled (ταράσσω) by the demons, and at times also, sobering up (ἀνανήφω) from the senselessness (ἀλογιστία) under them, to see a little of the truth. For again he adds: God must in no place in no way be left (ἀπολείπω), neither by day (μεθ᾿ ἡμέραν) nor by night (νύκτωρ), nor in public (ἐς κοινόν) nor privately (ἰδίᾳ), in every word (λόγος) and deed (ἔργον) continually (διηνεκῶς); but both with these and without (χωρίς), let the soul always be stretched (τείνω) toward God. I hear (ἀκούω) 'with these' as: with the public, and with every deed and every word. Then again, as if wrestling (παλαίω) in reasoning (λογισμός) against the frenzies / ecstasies (ἐκστάσεις) from the demons and being mostly conquered (νικάω), he adds and says: if things are so, what is the dreadful thing (τὸ δεινόν) in propitiating (εὐμενίζομαι) the rulers (ἄρχοντες) here, both the others and the potentates (δυνάσται) and kings (βασιλεῖς) among men, as not even these having been deemed worthy (ἀξιόω) of the things here without demonic strength (δαιμονία ἰσχύς)? In the things above he was bringing down, as far as in him, our soul to the demons; now he wants us to propitiate (ἐξευμενίζομαι) also the potentates and kings among men, of whom since life (βίος) and histories (ἱστορίαι) are full, I did not now think it necessary (ἀναγκαῖον) to set out (ἐκτίθημι) the examples (παραδείγματα).
pass_b_english: Celsus, I think, after all the words he spoke about demons who need the smoke of sacrifice and blood, as though turning to wickedness, sings a recantation and says that “we should rather believe that the demons need nothing and lack nothing, but take pleasure in those who act piously toward them.” If he thought this was true, he ought not to have set down those earlier words; he should have struck them out.

But human nature is not wholly abandoned by God and by the Truth, His only-begotten. That is why Celsus too spoke the truth in what he said about the smoke of sacrifice and the blood that demons crave; but again, by his own wickedness, he slid down into falsehood, and he likens the demons to men who do what is just in a perfectly just way, even if no one thanks them, and who do good to those who repay them with gratitude.

He seems to me to be confused on this subject: at one moment his ruling mind is troubled by the demons, and at another, coming back to his senses from the folly he suffers under them, he sees a little of the truth. For again he adds: “But God must not be forsaken anywhere or in any way, neither by day nor by night, neither in public nor in private, in every word and in every deed continually; indeed, both with these and apart from them, let the soul be always directed toward God.” I take “with these” to mean with public life, with every deed and with every word.

Then again, as though wrestling in his reasoning against the frenzies that come from the demons and being mostly overcome, he goes on to say: “If this is so, what is so dreadful in winning the favour of the rulers here, both the others and the princes and kings among men, since not even these have been granted their place in this world without the strength of demons?” Earlier, as far as it lay with him, he was dragging our soul down to the demons; now he wants us to win the favour of the princes and kings among men as well. Since life and the histories are full of examples of these men, I have not thought it necessary to set them out now.

choices.choice: Three Celsus quotations: (1) ‘we should rather believe ... act piously toward them’ (Origen frames it with ὅτι; kept in quotation marks as Celsus’s claim); (2) ‘But God must never ... toward God’; (3) ‘If this is so ... without the strength of demons?’. ὡσπερεὶ ἐπὶ μοχθηρίαν ἐρχόμενος παλινῳδίαν φησίν: παλινῳδίαν is taken as the object of φησίν (‘sings a recantation’), with ἐπὶ μοχθηρίαν ἐρχόμενος as ‘slipping back into wickedness’. Doubtful: ἐκεῖνα αὐτὸν μὴ τεθεικέναι, ταῦτα ἀπηλειφέναι has no connective; it is read as ‘not to have set down those earlier words, and [having set them down] to have struck them out’, with ἐκεῖνα and ταῦτα both meaning the earlier statements about blood and savour; a lost ἤ (‘or’) is possible. τῆς μονογενοῦς αὐτῷ ἀληθείας: ‘the Truth, His only-begotten’, a title of Christ drawing on John 14:6 and John 1:14, 18; not cited inline because it is a title, not a quotation. ἀνανήφων may echo 2 Timothy 2:26 (ἀνανήψωσιν), possible only, not cited. ἐκστάσεις rendered ‘frenzies’. ‘the rulers here’ (τοὺς τῇδε ἄρχοντας) keeps Celsus’s τῇδε (‘in this world’). The article αἱ before ἱστορίαι is Koetschau’s supplement (in parentheses in the source). Review: the clause τὰ ἀγαθὰ δὲ ποιοῦσι τοῖς ἀμειβομένοις τὸ εὐχάριστον could also make the demons the subject (‘and they do good to those who repay them with thanks’); the draft’s reading, which keeps it in the comparison with just men, is kept.
ἐπὶ μοχθηρίαν ἐρχόμενος: dropped added 'back' ('as though turning to wickedness')
Asyndeton ἐκεῖνα ... μὴ τεθεικέναι, ταῦτα ἀπηλειφέναι kept as two clauses with a semicolon instead of 'and'
οὐδαμῇ οὐδαμῶς 'never in any way' to 'not ... anywhere or in any way' (place and manner, not time)
τετάσθω 'stretched out toward God' (calque) to 'directed toward God'
